paper_sections.title: Damaged Insula Network Contributes to Depression in Parkinson’s Disease

description.value: The study investigated insula functional connectivity abnormalities in Parkinson’s disease and depression-related connectivity changes by comparing depressed PD patients, non-depressed PD patients, and normal controls.

design.value: Cross-sectional resting-state functional MRI study of two groups of PD patients, with and without depression, and age- and sex-matched normal controls.

source_definition.value: depressed PD patients, non-depressed PD patients, and normal controls

exclusion_criteria.value: cerebrovascular disorders, including a previous stroke, a history of seizure, hydrocephalus, an intracranial mass, a history of head injury, previous neurological surgery, or other neurological diseases; any current DSM-IV Axis I diagnosis other than MDD; treatment with antidepressants or other psychiatric therapy; dementia; unable to keep still during the MRI because of head motion

recruitment_method.value: recruited from the Department of Neurology, Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University

diagnostic_system.value: UK PD Brain Bank criteria; Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th Edition criteria (DSM-IV)

diagnostic_instrument.value: Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS); Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD); Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA); Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE)

medication_status.value: No treatment with antidepressants or other psychiatric therapy

description.value: Seventeen normal controls matched for age and sex

task_description.value: Subjects were instructed to relax with their eyes closed without falling asleep, and without directed systematic thought.

instructions.value: Relax with their eyes closed without falling asleep, and without directed systematic thought.

description.value: Echo planar imaging sequence; flip angle = 90°, FOV = 240 × 240 mm2, matrix = 64 × 64, slice thickness = 5 mm, slice gap = 1 mm, 23 interleaved axial slices. A total of 185 resting-state BOLD images were acquired from each subject.
3-D GRE T1-weighted sequence; TR/TE = 5.14 ms/1.17 ms, FOV = 240 × 240 mm2, matrix = 256 × 256, slice thickness = 1.2 mm, no gap, 124 sagittal slices.

The first 10 images were excluded; remaining images were slice-time corrected, realigned, nuisance-regressed, normalized into standard space using DARTEL, resampled to 3 × 3 × 3 mm, smoothed with a 6-mm Gaussian kernel, linearly detrended, and bandpass filtered at 0.01~0.1 Hz. Framewise displacement was used to censor time points with FD > 0.5 mm; subjects with fewer than 130 remaining time points were excluded.

software.value: Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI (DPARSF); Resting-State fMRI Data Analysis Toolkit (REST V1.8); DARTEL

steps.value: Exclude first 10 images; slice timing correction; realignment; regression of Friston-24 head motion parameters and white matter and CSF signals using CompCor; normalization using DARTEL; resampling to 3 × 3 × 3 mm; 6-mm Gaussian smoothing; linear detrending; 0.01~0.1 Hz bandpass filtering; framewise-displacement scrubbing at FD > 0.5 mm; exclude subjects with fewer than 130 remaining time points.

model_settings.value: Correlation was calculated between the average time series within the insula ROIs and other brain areas; connectivity maps were transformed to Z maps using Fisher r-to-z transformation.

estimator.value: Pearson’s correlation with Fisher r-to-z transformation

model_settings.value: Age and sex were used as covariates.
